Chronological order arranges items by when they happened — earlier before later — so the sequence itself is the index.
Journals, logs, and feeds use it so a reader can ask what happened next?

In this garden, journaling is deliberately chronological; knowledge gardening is not. Related pages should sit near each other the way a Graph/Database clusters neighbors, not in the order they were filed.
Other orders in the garden answer different questions:
Alpha/Bet/ic/al/Order — by letters of the alphabet, for human-readable lists of words.
Other orders in the garden answer different questions:
Lexicographic/Order — by the full character repertoire of a name, including digits and punctuation; the order s actually use.
Other orders in the garden answer different questions:
Time is the key — the sort key is a date or timestamp, not a title.
Precision follows knowledge — year, month, or day per Logseq/Date; do not fake a day when only a year is known.
Sequence is not proximity — two notes written on consecutive days may be about unrelated things; chronology does not cluster by topic.
A journal page journals/YYYY_MM_DD.md and a wikilink in the YYYY-MM-DD Day shape are chronological addresses.
Entity paths that embed <YY>/<MM> (blogs, podcasts, books) use chronology as a secondary key after creator and type, so works still cluster by who made them.
A blog post path Person/<Name>/Blog/<YY>/<MM>/<slug> — dated, but nested under the author.
A series path that also uses an ordinal — publication year and reading order can diverge; Logseq/Entity/Series prefers the ordinal when the published sequence numbers its parts.
"Filing by date keeps related things together" — False unless the relatedness is the date (a trip, a conference). Topic clusters need a graph-like layout instead.
"Alphabetical and chronological are the two orders" — Incomplete; filesystem sort is Lexicographic/Order, which is a generalization of Alpha/Bet/ic/al/Order and is not a time order.

In biology, a clade is a group made up of one common ancestor and all of its descendants. Biologists also call it a monophyletic group.
From Ancient Greek kládos, "shoot, branch". The biologist Julian Huxley coined the word in 1957, in the Nature paper "The Three Types of Evolutionary Process".
Clades nest inside one another, because each branch of the tree of life splits into smaller branches.

A group that leaves out some descendants of its common ancestor is paraphyletic. The traditional class Reptilia is the usual example: it holds the last common ancestor of reptiles and its descendants, except the birds.
Clades are the basic unit of cladistics, the approach to taxonomy that most fields of biology now use.

In the entity system described on Logseq/Entity, the clade of Logseq/Entity/Person would be Person together with every entity that is a kind of person, such as Logseq/Entity/Person/Maker/Music and Logseq/Entity/Person/Knowledge Gardener. A published Claude artifact can be installed as its own app on your computer. It gets a dedicated window, an icon in your app launcher, and no browser tab or address bar.
The artifact is a web page at a claude.ai URL, so the feature comes from the browser's PWA install, not from a Claude-specific installer.
On the artifact page, the title menu (the name with a chevron, top left) lists Export, Copy as Markdown, Install artifact, and Rename.
Install artifact opens Chrome's "Install app" dialog: "Access this site in a dedicated window on your computer". It shows the artifact name followed by "Claude artifact" and the domain claude.ai.
Next goes to a second dialog showing the icon moving into a Chrome Apps folder. Install finishes it.
A confirmation offers Show in Finder and Open tab in app.
A standalone window for one artifact, separate from your browser tabs and from the Claude app.
A launcher icon: Start menu on Windows, Launchpad and Spotlight on macOS, as listed by web.dev.
Entries in the OS app switcher and app search, with the option to pin to the taskbar on Windows.
Windows works. Chrome and Edge both install PWAs on Windows, macOS, Linux, and Chromebooks, per web.dev.
In Chrome: More (three dots) → Cast, save, and share → Install page as app, or the install icon at the right end of the address bar. See Google's Chrome Help.
In Edge: the App available icon in the address bar, then Install. The app lands in the Start menu and taskbar, and appears under Windows Apps & features. See Microsoft's Edge PWA guide.
Edge on Windows can also start the app when you sign in (edge://apps → More options → Auto-start on device login).
The browser-level install is documented for Edge. Whether claude.ai shows the Install artifact menu item in Edge is undocumented.
Edge has one documented gap: PWAs do not survive logoff in FSLogix virtual-desktop profiles.
Safari on macOS does not support installability (web.dev). Use Chrome or Edge.
Firefox on desktop is not covered by those sources.
An app cannot be installed twice in the same browser.
Chrome: open chrome://apps to see installed apps, create shortcuts, or set launch at sign-in. To remove one, open it and choose More → Uninstall.
Edge: edge://apps, or Windows Add or remove programs.
Answer/Official for the browser mechanism: the Chrome, Edge, and web.dev pages linked above.
No Anthropic Help Center article describes Install artifact. The article What are artifacts and how do I use them? covers viewing, editing, sharing, and exporting, and says nothing on installing.
The dialogs in the screenshots are Chrome's own PWA install flow with Claude's name and icon filled in.
